subject: english-literature
topicDisplay: Non Exam Assessment Literature Post 1900 Close Reading And Comparative Essay
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: 'Dramatic irony' occurs when:
options: the chorus comments on the action
the audience knows something a character on stage does not
a character speaks in verse while others speak in prose
the play breaks the fourth wall
questions.explain: Dramatic irony arises from the gap between the audience's knowledge and a character's ignorance of it.

questions.q: A structurally aware reading of a novel would consider:
options: the author's choice of typeface
the colour of the book's cover
how the ordering of events, pacing, chapter divisions and shifts in time shape the reader's understanding
only the meaning of isolated metaphors
questions.explain: Structure concerns how a text is organised over time, and how that organisation guides response.

questions.q: A 'feminist' reading of a canonical play would most characteristically interrogate:
options: the unconscious of the playwright alone
the iambic substitutions in the verse
how the text constructs, constrains or resists gender roles and female agency
the rules of classical unity
questions.explain: Feminist criticism examines representations of gender, patriarchal structures and the agency afforded to women in the text.

questions.q: A 'psychoanalytic' (Freudian) reading would typically attend to:
options: the text's fidelity to historical fact
the rhythm and metre of the verse alone
the economic base determining the cultural superstructure
the unconscious, repression, desire and symbolic expressions of inner conflict
questions.explain: Psychoanalytic criticism reads texts for unconscious drives, repression and symbolic enactments of psychic conflict.

questions.q: At A-level, AO1 chiefly assesses a candidate's ability to:
options: analyse the influence of contexts on a text
explore how different readers interpret a text
analyse the writer's use of form, structure and language
articulate an informed, personal response using a coherent, accurate critical argument and terminology
questions.explain: AO1 rewards a coherent, well-written argument expressed in accurate critical terminology with relevant textual support.

questions.q: An 'ecocritical' reading would be most interested in:
options: the text's depiction of class struggle
the relationship between the text, the non-human world and the environment
the gendered power relations within the household
the repressed desires of the central characters
questions.explain: Ecocriticism examines how literature represents nature, place and humanity's relationship with the environment.

questions.q: The 'connotation' of a word is:
options: its position in the sentence
its number of syllables
its literal dictionary definition
the associations and overtones it carries beyond its literal sense
questions.explain: Connotation refers to the implied associations a word evokes, as opposed to its denotative literal meaning.

questions.q: Which AO is most directly engaged when a student discusses how a poem's original readers would have understood its references to colonial trade?
options: AO3
AO1
AO4
AO2
questions.explain: AO3 assesses understanding of the contexts in which texts are written and received.

questions.q: A response arguing that a text 'cannot be reduced to a single meaning' and surveying competing readings is engaging most strongly with:
options: AO1 only
AO2 only
AO4
AO5
questions.explain: Acknowledging multiple, competing interpretations is the core of AO5.

questions.q: A 'reader-response' approach holds that meaning is:
options: irrelevant to literary study
determined solely by the historical context of composition
produced in the interaction between the text and the reader's act of interpretation
fixed entirely by the author's stated intention
questions.explain: Reader-response criticism locates meaning in the transaction between text and reader rather than in the author alone.

questions.q: 'Framing' as a structural device most often refers to:
options: a story enclosed within another narrative that introduces and concludes it
the alphabetical ordering of chapters
the use of iambic pentameter throughout
the metaphors clustered in a single stanza
questions.explain: A frame narrative encloses an inner tale, often shaping how the reader judges its reliability and meaning.

questions.q: 'Foregrounding' in stylistic analysis means:
options: placing a scene at the front of the play
describing the background setting
summarising the plot's opening
making a linguistic feature prominent through deviation or repetition so it draws attention
questions.explain: Foregrounding makes language conspicuous through patterning or deviation, directing the reader's interpretive attention.

questions.q: A 'new historicist' reading of a literary text would most characteristically:
options: judge the text purely by its formal elegance and unity
treat the text as one of many cultural documents circulating within and shaping the power relations of its period
focus only on the reader's emotional response
read the text as a timeless expression of universal human nature
questions.explain: New historicism situates a text among the period's other discourses, reading literature and history as mutually constitutive.

questions.q: When a critic's view is quoted in an essay, the most analytically rigorous use of it is to:
options: treat it as a position to be tested, endorsed or challenged against the text
place it at the start to replace the student's own argument
accept it as the final, authoritative answer
quote it without further comment
questions.explain: Critics' views (AO5) should be deployed as debatable positions that the student evaluates through their own reading.

questions.q: The most sophisticated use of a critical quotation is to:
options: ignore it entirely
engage with it dialectically, qualifying or contesting it through close textual evidence
agree with it uncritically
place it at the end as a flourish
questions.explain: AO5 rewards a critical dialogue with other readings, tested against the student's own analysis of the text.

questions.q: AO2 is best satisfied when a student:
options: summarises three critics' opinions
describes the writer's life and times
lists the events of the plot in order
analyses how specific choices of form, structure and language create meaning and effect
questions.explain: AO2 rewards close analysis of the writer's craft and the effects of formal, structural and linguistic choices.

questions.q: A 'Marxist' reading of a novel would be most likely to foreground:
options: the sublime grandeur of the landscape
the author's use of assonance
the protagonist's Oedipal anxieties
class, labour, ideology and the material conditions shaping the characters
questions.explain: Marxist criticism analyses class conflict, ideology and how material and economic forces shape texts and characters.

questions.q: Which sentence best demonstrates an integrated, analytical (rather than descriptive) point?
options: The clipped monosyllables and end-stopped lines enact the speaker's controlled rage, refusing the release that fuller rhythm would allow.
This passage is about anger and conflict.
The character is angry in this scene.
Anger is a theme that appears in the text.
questions.explain: Analytical writing links a precise technique to its effect on meaning, rather than merely naming a theme.

questions.q: In a comparative essay, the strongest approach to comparison is to:
options: build an integrated argument in which texts are set against each other around shared concerns and differing methods
note only that the texts share a theme
summarise text one fully, then text two, with no cross-reference
compare the authors' biographies in detail
questions.explain: High-level comparison interweaves texts around a thesis, analysing similarities and differences in method and effect.

questions.q: Which is the best example of using context (AO3) analytically rather than as 'bolted-on' background?
options: Showing how the poem's anxieties about industrialisation shape its imagery of the polluted river
A paragraph narrating the author's biography before discussing the text
Listing the dates of the period at the essay's start
Stating that the text was written in the nineteenth century
questions.explain: Context is used well when it illuminates specific textual choices rather than sitting as detached background.

questions.q: The term 'narrative voice' refers to:
options: the literal volume at which a poem should be read
the moral message of a text
the persona and perspective through which a story is told
the metre of a passage of verse
questions.explain: Narrative voice denotes the constructed perspective and persona delivering the narration, distinct from the author.

questions.q: 'Tone' in a literary text refers to:
options: the writer's or speaker's attitude towards the subject, conveyed through diction and form
the historical setting
the literal sound of words read aloud
the moral lesson of the work
questions.explain: Tone is the implied attitude or stance of the speaker towards subject or audience, signalled by linguistic choices.

questions.q: In close reading, attending to 'syntax' means examining:
options: the choice of individual words for connotation
the arrangement and ordering of words into sentence structures and their effects
the rhyme scheme of a stanza
the historical period of the text
questions.explain: Syntax concerns sentence structure and word order, whose patterning shapes pace, emphasis and meaning.

questions.q: A 'motif' differs from a 'symbol' in that a motif is:
options: a recurring image, idea or device whose repetition builds significance across a text
a figure of speech comparing two unlike things
always a physical object
a single image used only once for emphasis
questions.explain: A motif gains its meaning through recurrence, whereas a symbol stands for something beyond itself at the point of use.

questions.q: In analysing a poem, identifying a 'volta' means recognising:
options: the repeated refrain at each stanza's end
the poem's opening invocation
the rhyme scheme of the final couplet
a turn or shift in thought, argument or tone, often in a sonnet
questions.explain: A volta is a turn in a poem's argument or mood, classically marking the shift between octave and sestet in a sonnet.

questions.q: A 'post-colonial' reading is most concerned with:
options: the recurrence of a single image
the purging of pity and fear in the audience
metre and rhyme scheme
representations of empire, the colonised 'other', hybridity and cultural power
questions.explain: Post-colonial criticism interrogates how texts construct empire, the colonised subject and relations of cultural power.

questions.q: An 'unreliable narrator' is one whose:
options: narration is consistently omniscient and authoritative
story is told entirely in the present tense
perspective shifts between several characters
account the reader is invited to question because their credibility is compromised
questions.explain: An unreliable narrator's version of events is undermined by gaps, bias or self-deception that the reader must read against.

questions.q: When two texts are compared, a 'point of divergence' is most valuable when it:
options: proves one text is superior
shows the texts are completely unrelated
repeats a similarity already noted
reveals how each writer handles a shared concern differently, illuminating both
questions.explain: Productive comparison uses difference to sharpen understanding of each text's distinctive method and meaning.

questions.q: In narrative theory, 'free indirect discourse' is best defined as:
options: an authorial commentary that judges the characters explicitly
a character's thoughts rendered in the third person yet inflected with that character's own idiom and feeling
a first-person narrator addressing the reader directly
direct speech reported within quotation marks
questions.explain: Free indirect discourse blends the narrator's third-person report with a character's voice, blurring the line between the two.

questions.q: A response that explores how a text can sustain feminist, Marxist and psychoanalytic readings is primarily demonstrating which assessment objective?
options: AO3
AO5
AO2
AO4
questions.explain: AO5 rewards engagement with different interpretations, including the application of distinct critical lenses.
